rv.q: Hilarious and hurting — and tenderly delivered by Siobhán McSweeney— it should become the stuff of a thousand auditions.
It’s also a profoundly accurate account of the world we live in today...
A play fit, then, for the summer silly season and yet one that resonates in a more lasting, chilling way with the madnesses of our strife-riven age.
Ultimately, though, it’s more frustrating than likeable.
After almost two hours in its company I was none the wiser.
But overall: Pity is just a shame.
While the creation of mess can make for gleeful theatre, here it just feels relentless and, even less forgivably, kind of boring.
His play comes across in performance as an apocalyptic, prodigally wasteful cartoon.
And, for me, it sums the play up, some fantastical sequences but also some frustrating treading of water.
While the production is pretty glorious in all its extravagance, the text could do with a clearer voice and a subtler approach to become an enticing watch.
Horribly adolescent and wilfully immature, I loved it and loathed it in equal regards.

The whole thing comes across as absurd and quite possibly absurdist, featuring elements drawn from a number of different theatrical styles in an evening directed by Sam Pritchard that will undoubtedly prove a delight to those who get it and pure torture to everybody else.
Mullarkey’s last play ST GEORGE AND THE DRAGON was one of the worst plays I’ve ever seen at the National, now PITY is the worst thing I’ve ever seen at the Royal Court.
Pity is, probably one of the best shows I have ever seen.
Prepare to have your senses heightened and your imagination stretched, with this weird and wonderful piece of contemporary theatre.
But Mullarkey’s sensibility is pretty nihilistic.
One of the most distinctive plays this year, Pity is a typical Royal Court boundary-pusher that will divide audience opinion with its surrealism and occasional smugness.
The great pity is that Mullarkey's play is so unfunny and such an apocalyptic comic strip bore.
Pity is about as polarising as a mainstream play can be, and I’m afraid I’m on the end of the pole that says “avoid at all costs”.

cn.t: A divisive absurdist fable that polarizes audiences with its bonkers apocalyptic vision of Middle England. Critics split between finding it ridiculous fun and frustratingly wasteful, though most agree the opening village green spectacle impresses.
